CVaR Deep Optimal Stopping

Yechan Jeong Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: yechan@snu.ac.kr    Youngjoon Hong Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: hongyj@snu.ac.kr
Abstract

Risk-sensitive optimal stopping is useful when poor stopping outcomes carry substantial costs, as in option exercise, sequential medical treatment, and safety-critical control. A natural objective is Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the stopped reward. We develop a theoretical framework and algorithm for CVaR deep optimal stopping. The framework and algorithm address four difficulties in applying risk-sensitive reinforcement learning to optimal stopping: state augmentation, score-function pathology, blindness to success, and dependence on auxiliary networks. We isolate three structural properties of optimal stopping: single-point reward, action-independent dynamics, and sum-zero gradient. We exploit these properties to establish Markov optimality without state augmentation and derive a pathwise gradient estimator. Under bounded policy derivatives, the pathwise estimator has bounded second moments near deterministic policies, avoiding the divergence that can occur with score-function estimators. Building on this framework, we propose DIOS (Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping) to address the remaining two difficulties. A per-time-step soft penalty combined with tail-level annealing mitigates blindness to success. Estimating the reward quantile directly from each batch removes the need for an auxiliary critic. For a fixed tail level, we establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee under regularity assumptions along the training iterates. Across the 24 main Bermudan max-call configurations, DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time among the tested CVaR baselines.

1 Introduction

Risk-sensitive deep optimal stopping.

Risk-sensitive optimal stopping is useful when poor stopping outcomes carry substantial costs, as in option exercise, sequential medical treatment, and safety-critical control. Maximizing expected reward alone may give insufficient weight to adverse stopping outcomes. We study the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the stopped reward, which measures the average reward over a chosen fraction of the worst outcomes [21, 22].

Coherent risk measure and CVaR.

A coherent risk measure satisfies monotonicity, translation invariance, positive homogeneity, and subadditivity [1]. The negative of lower-tail CVaR is a coherent risk measure for rewards [22]. We choose CVaR to optimize the average reward over a prescribed fraction of the worst stopping outcomes. The Rockafellar–Uryasev representation decomposes CVaR optimal stopping into an outer optimization over a scalar variable and an inner risk-neutral stopping problem. Standard stopping theory and deep optimal stopping methods can therefore be applied to the inner stopping problem.

Deep optimal stopping.

The Snell envelope characterizes risk-neutral optimal stopping [24], and the regression-based approach of Longstaff and Schwartz [16] provides a method for American option pricing. Deep learning is used to address the curse of dimensionality in optimal stopping. Becker et al. [3] introduced deep optimal stopping, a backward-induction method that parameterizes each per-step stopping probability with a neural network and trains the networks in backward order. Neural-network regression methods approximate continuation values [15, 11]. Other methods jointly optimize stopping probabilities across time [4, 8], with shared policy parameters in Damera Venkata and Bhattacharyya [8]. Language models have also been applied to stopping decisions in sales conversations [19]. We study CVaR deep optimal stopping, replacing expected-reward maximization with lower-tail CVaR maximization.

Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning.

For CVaR objectives and constraints, Bäuerle and Ott [2], Chow and Ghavamzadeh [6], and Chow et al. [7] obtain Bellman recursions by augmenting the state with risk or cumulative-reward variables. Tamar et al. [25] derive a score-function CVaR policy-gradient (CVaR-PG) estimator. Methods for improving sample efficiency in CVaR policy optimization modify sampling, policy parameterization, or gradient estimation. Greenberg et al. [10] pair a soft-risk schedule with a cross-entropy environment sampler. Luo et al. [18] combine a risk-averse policy with a risk-neutral policy trained via Implicit Q-Learning [14]. Kim and Min [13] weight individual costs by predicted tail probabilities from a separate network. Mead et al. [20] compute policy gradients from trajectory returns capped at a value updated during training. Luo and Delage [17] mix the CVaR-PG gradient with a quantile-gradient term computed by an auxiliary quantile critic. These CVaR methods can be applied to optimal stopping, a finite-horizon MDP with a binary stop/continue action and action-independent state process. Applying risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) to optimal stopping raises four difficulties.

Four structural problems of risk-sensitive RL.

  • (P1)

    State augmentation. Static CVaR objectives can be time-inconsistent [23]. Existing CVaR-MDP methods obtain Bellman recursions by adding variables for accumulated costs to the state [2, 6, 7].

  • (P2)

    Score-function pathology. Near deterministic policies, the second moment of the trajectory-level score-function estimator can diverge or vanish, depending on the policy parameterization. Several methods retain a score-function CVaR-PG component [10, 18, 17].

  • (P3)

    Blindness to success. The CVaR-PG gradient estimator assigns zero weight to trajectories with rewards above the estimated quantile. The CVaR-PG gradient estimate can also vanish when the sampled lower-tail rewards coincide [10, 17].

  • (P4)

    Dependence on auxiliary networks. Several methods use learned tail probabilities, values, or quantiles in policy updates [13, 18, 17]. The auxiliary networks are trained on data generated by the policy.

Optimal stopping addresses (P1) and permits a pathwise treatment of (P2). DIOS addresses (P3) and removes the auxiliary critic in (P4).

Framework: addressing (P1) and (P2).

The single-point reward (S1) and the envelope reduction give Markov optimality without state augmentation. Action-independent dynamics (S2) permit differentiation of the conditional stopping probabilities without a trajectory score term. The sum-zero gradient (S3) makes the pathwise gradient invariant to a common shift of the transformed rewards. Under the policy-derivative bounds, pathwise gradient moments remain bounded near deterministic policies.

DIOS and convergence: addressing (P3) and (P4).

We propose Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping (DIOS), a pathwise algorithm for CVaR optimal stopping. A per-time-step soft penalty allows rewards at other stopping times to contribute even when the sampled stopping reward exceeds the estimated quantile. Training starts with a tail level of 11, then gradually reduces the tail level to its target. Direct quantile estimation from each batch removes the auxiliary critic. Theorem 4.2 gives a finite-time best-iterate stationarity guarantee when the analyzed iterates remain in a domain satisfying the regularity assumptions.

Contributions.

  • •

    We exploit (S1)–(S3) to develop a CVaR optimal stopping framework addressing (P1) and (P2). We establish the envelope reduction (Proposition 3.1) and prove Markov optimality without state augmentation (Theorem 3.3).

  • •

    We derive a pathwise gradient estimator (Lemma 3.6) and bound its second moments under the policy-derivative and reward-moment assumptions (Lemma 3.9). We compare pathwise and score-function gradients near deterministic policies (Theorem 3.10).

  • •

    We propose Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping (DIOS, Algorithm 1). DIOS combines a per-time-step soft penalty with tail-level annealing to mitigate (P3). Direct quantile estimation removes the auxiliary critic in (P4). At a fixed tail level, we establish a finite-time best-iterate stationarity guarantee under the regularity and parameter-domain conditions of Theorem 4.2.

  • •

    We demonstrate across 24 Bermudan max-call configurations that DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time among the tested CVaR baselines [25, 13, 18, 20, 17].

2 Deep optimal stopping and CVaR

2.1 Deep optimal stopping

Setup.

We work in the finite-horizon, discrete-time, model-free setting. Fix a probability space (Ω,ℱ,P)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P) and a finite horizon T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}. Let (St)t=0T(S_{t})_{t=0}^{T} be an ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued Markov process and (ℱt)t=0T(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t=0}^{T} its natural filtration, ℱt:=σ⁡(S0,…,St)\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma(S_{0},\dots,S_{t}). Define Rt:=gt​(St)R_{t}:=g_{t}(S_{t}), where gt:ℝd→ℝ+g_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is Borel-measurable. The joint distribution of (S0,…,ST)(S_{0},\ldots,S_{T}) is unknown and accessed only through samples. Appendix A discusses the assumptions for the Bermudan max-call experiments in Section 5.

Assumption 2.1 (Integrability).

Rt∈L1​(P)R_{t}\in L^{1}(P) for every t∈{0,…,T}t\in\{0,\dots,T\}.

V∗:=supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[Rτ].V^{*}\;:=\;\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[R_{\tau}\right]. (1)

VT:=RT,Vt:=max⁡(Rt,𝔼⁡[Vt+1∣ℱt])for ​t<T.V_{T}:=R_{T},\quad V_{t}:=\max\!\left(R_{t},\ \mathbb{E}[V_{t+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\right)\quad\text{for }t<T. (2)

Assumption 2.1 ensures that VtV_{t} is integrable for every t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T. For t<Tt<T, an optimal rule stops when the immediate reward RtR_{t} satisfies Rt≥𝔼⁡[Vt+1∣ℱt]R_{t}\geq\mathbb{E}[V_{t+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}] and continues otherwise, with a forced stop at TT. Let ϕ=(ϕ0,…,ϕT)\phi=(\phi_{0},\ldots,\phi_{T}) consist of Borel functions ϕt:ℝd→[0,1]\phi_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to[0,1] with ϕT≡1\phi_{T}\equiv 1. Three structural properties of optimal stopping.

We exploit the following three properties of the stopping formulation.

  • (S1)

    Single-point reward. The reward Rτ=gτ​(Sτ)R_{\tau}=g_{\tau}(S_{\tau}) is realized at the single time index τ\tau, in contrast to cumulative-return MDPs where rewards ∑trt\sum_{t}r_{t} are summed over the trajectory.

  • (S2)

    Action-independent dynamics. The state process (St)t=0T(S_{t})_{t=0}^{T} evolves under a transition kernel that does not depend on the stopping action.

  • (S3)

    Sum-zero gradient. Parameterize the policy by θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, where Θ⊂ℝp\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} is open, and assume each θ↦ψtθ\theta\mapsto\psi_{t}^{\theta} is differentiable PP-a.s. Since (5) holds for every θ\theta, differentiating in θ\theta yields

    ∑t=0T∇θψtθ= 0P​-a.s.\sum_{t=0}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta}\;=\;0\qquad P\text{-a.s.}

2.2 CVaR optimal stopping

Fix β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). For X∈L1​(P)X\in L^{1}(P), define the lower β\beta-quantile by VaRβ​(X):=inf{x:P⁡(X≤x)≥β}\mathrm{VaR}_{\beta}(X):=\inf\{x:P(X\leq x)\geq\beta\}. Define the Conditional Value at Risk by

CVaRβ​(X):=1β​∫0βVaRu​(X)​𝑑u.\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(X)\;:=\;\tfrac{1}{\beta}\int_{0}^{\beta}\mathrm{VaR}_{u}(X)\,du. (7)

Define CVaR1​(X):=𝔼​[X]\mathrm{CVaR}_{1}(X):=\mathbb{E}[X]. Smaller β\beta focuses the objective on a smaller fraction of the lowest outcomes. The Rockafellar-Uryasev variational form expresses CVaR as a one-dimensional supremum [22],

CVaRβ​(X)=supν∈ℝ{ν−1β​𝔼​[(ν−X)+]},\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(X)\;=\;\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}\Bigl\{\nu\;-\;\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbb{E}[(\nu-X)^{+}]\Bigr\}, (8)

attained at ν∗=VaRβ​(X)\nu^{*}=\mathrm{VaR}_{\beta}(X) for 0<β<10<\beta<1. The quantity (ν−X)+=max⁡{ν−X,0}(\nu-X)^{+}=\max\{\nu-X,0\} measures the shortfall below ν\nu. Replacing the expectation in (1) with CVaR yields the CVaR optimal stopping value

Vβ∗:=supτ∈𝒯CVaRβ​(Rτ).V^{*}_{\beta}\;:=\;\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\,\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(R_{\tau}). (9)

3 CVaR within the deep optimal stopping framework

Building on the Rockafellar–Uryasev envelope reduction, we establish Markov optimality without state augmentation and derive a pathwise gradient formula.

3.1 Envelope reduction

Proofs are given in Appendix B.

Proposition 3.1 (CVaR envelope reduction).

Under Assumption 2.1 and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1),

Vβ∗=supν∈ℝ{ν+1β​supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[−(ν−Rτ)+]},V^{*}_{\beta}\;=\;\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}\Bigl\{\nu\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[-(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}]\Bigr\}, (10)

and there exist ν∗∈ℝ\nu^{*}\in\mathbb{R} and τ∗∈𝒯\tau^{*}\in\mathcal{T} with ν∗=VaRβ​(Rτ∗)\nu^{*}=\mathrm{VaR}_{\beta}(R_{\tau^{*}}) jointly realizing the supremum.

Proposition 3.1 separates an outer maximization over the scalar ν\nu from an inner risk-neutral stopping problem at fixed ν\nu. Define the per-step soft penalty R~tν:=−1β​(ν−Rt)+\tilde{R}^{\nu}_{t}:=-\tfrac{1}{\beta}(\nu-R_{t})^{+}. For the parameterized stopping policies ϕθ\phi^{\theta}, define the objective for the inner maximization over θ\theta by

J(ν)​(θ):=𝔼⁡[∑t=0Tψtθ⋅R~tν].J^{(\nu)}(\theta)\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\psi_{t}^{\theta}\cdot\tilde{R}^{\nu}_{t}\right]. (11)

For fixed ν\nu, the Snell-envelope recursion and stopping-policy representation in Section 2.1 apply with RtR_{t} replaced by R~tν\tilde{R}_{t}^{\nu}. Appendix I extends the outer–inner decomposition to an optimized certainty equivalent objective.

3.2 Markov optimality without augmentation

Applying CVaR recursively at each time generally changes the static CVaR objective [23]. CVaR-MDP methods instead obtain Bellman recursions by adding variables for accumulated costs to the state [2, 6, 7].

Definition 3.2 (Markov stopping time).

Define a stopping time τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} to be Markov if there exist Borel sets D0,…,DT⊆ℝdD_{0},\ldots,D_{T}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with DT=ℝdD_{T}=\mathbb{R}^{d} such that τ=inf{t≥0:St∈Dt}\tau=\inf\{t\geq 0:S_{t}\in D_{t}\} PP-a.s.

Theorem 3.3 (Markov optimality without augmentation).

Under Assumption 2.1 and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), there exist ν∗∈ℝ\nu^{*}\in\mathbb{R} and a Markov stopping time τ∗∈𝒯\tau^{*}\in\mathcal{T} such that

Vβ∗=ν∗+1β​𝔼​[−(ν∗−Rτ∗)+].V^{*}_{\beta}\;=\;\nu^{*}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[-(\nu^{*}-R_{\tau^{*}})^{+}\right].
Remark 3.4.

For fixed ν∗\nu^{*}, (S1) makes the transformed reward −(ν∗−gt​(St))+-(\nu^{*}-g_{t}(S_{t}))^{+} a function of the current state and time. By the Markov property, each conditional expectation in the Snell-envelope recursion is a function of tt and StS_{t}, with no additional dependence on S0,…,St−1S_{0},\ldots,S_{t-1}.

For fixed ν\nu, we show that pathwise gradient second moments remain uniformly bounded under bounded policy derivatives, whereas score-function second moments can diverge as stopping probabilities approach zero.

Let τ=τθ\tau=\tau_{\theta}. For t<Tt<T, let at=𝟏{Ut≤ϕtθ(St)}a_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{U_{t}\leq\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t})\} and define πθ​(at∣St):=(ϕtθ​(St))at​(1−ϕtθ​(St))1−at\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid S_{t}):=(\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t}))^{a_{t}}(1-\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t}))^{1-a_{t}}. Define the likelihood of the sampled actions up to τ\tau, conditional on (S0,…,ST)(S_{0},\ldots,S_{T}), by πθ​(τ):=∏t=0min⁡{τ,T−1}πθ​(at∣St)\pi_{\theta}(\tau):=\prod_{t=0}^{\min\{\tau,T-1\}}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid S_{t}). For comparison with existing score-function CVaR policy-gradient methods [25], define the loss for automatic differentiation at fixed ν\nu by

Lscore​(θ):=−𝔼⁡[sg⁡[R~τν]⋅log⁡πθ​(τ)].L_{\rm score}(\theta)\;:=\;-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathrm{sg}\!\left[\tilde{R}^{\nu}_{\tau}\right]\cdot\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau)\right].

∇^​Lscore​(θ):=−R~τν​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(τ),∇θLscore​(θ):=𝔼⁡[∇^​Lscore​(θ)].\hat{\nabla}L_{\rm score}(\theta):=-\tilde{R}^{\nu}_{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(\tau),\qquad\nabla_{\theta}L_{\rm score}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}L_{\rm score}(\theta)].

Under Assumptions 2.1 and 3.5, −∇θLscore​(θ)=∇θJ(ν)​(θ)-\nabla_{\theta}L_{\rm score}(\theta)=\nabla_{\theta}J^{(\nu)}(\theta). For the single-trajectory comparison B=1B=1, ∇^​L​(θ)\hat{\nabla}L(\theta) sums over all candidate stopping times, whereas ∇^​Lscore​(θ)\hat{\nabla}L_{\rm score}(\theta) uses the reward at the sampled stopping time τ\tau.

Theorem 3.10 (Bounded pathwise second moments and score-function divergence).

Under Assumptions 2.1, 3.5, and 3.8, fix ν∈ℝ\nu\in\mathbb{R} and a sequence (θn)⊂Θ(\theta_{n})\subset\Theta. Let B=1B=1. Suppose there exist t∗∈{0,…,T−1}t^{*}\in\{0,\dots,T-1\}, ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0, and an event A∈σ⁡(St∗)A\in\sigma(S_{t^{*}}) with P⁡(A)>0P(A)>0 such that ϕt∗θn​(St∗)→0\phi_{t^{*}}^{\theta_{n}}(S_{t^{*}})\to 0 on AA. (a)\displaystyle\text{(a)} infninfω∈A‖∇θϕt∗θn​(St∗​(ω))‖>0,\displaystyle\inf_{n}\inf_{\omega\in A}\|\nabla_{\theta}\phi_{t^{*}}^{\theta_{n}}(S_{t^{*}}(\omega))\|>0,

𝔼⁡[‖∇^​Lscore​(θn)‖2]→∞,supn𝔼⁡[‖∇^​L​(θn)‖2]<∞.\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{\nabla}L_{\rm score}(\theta_{n})\|^{2}]\to\infty,\qquad\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}[\|\hat{\nabla}L(\theta_{n})\|^{2}]<\infty.
Remark 3.11 (Sigmoid policies).

We implement the proposed algorithm, DIOS, using sigmoid policies. Fix ν∈ℝ\nu\in\mathbb{R}, let B=1B=1, and let (θn)⊂Θ(\theta_{n})\subset\Theta. Assume that the logit gradients are uniformly bounded in nn, tt, and the state. Then condition (a) of Theorem 3.10 fails if ϕt∗θn​(St∗)→0\phi_{t^{*}}^{\theta_{n}}(S_{t^{*}})\to 0. Under Assumptions 2.1, 3.5, and 3.8, if ϕtθn​(St)\phi_{t}^{\theta_{n}}(S_{t}) converges almost surely to 00 or 11 for every t<Tt<T, then ∇^​Lscore​(θn)→L20\hat{\nabla}L_{\rm score}(\theta_{n})\xrightarrow{L^{2}}0 and ∇^​L​(θn)→L20\hat{\nabla}L(\theta_{n})\xrightarrow{L^{2}}0, as proved in Appendix B.

4 Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping

DIOS (Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping) combines a per-time-step soft penalty with tail-level annealing. DIOS estimates the reward quantile directly from each batch without an auxiliary critic. Section 4.3 gives a finite-time stationarity guarantee for the fixed-tail-level update.

4.1 Blindness to success

CVaR-PG [25] estimates the gradient of CVaRβ​(Rτθ)\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(R_{\tau_{\theta}}) using a trajectory score. On each of BB independent state trajectories ii, let τθ(i)\tau_{\theta}^{(i)} be the stopping time generated by ϕθ\phi^{\theta}, and let πθ(i)\pi_{\theta}^{(i)} denote the action likelihood defined in Section 3.3, evaluated on trajectory ii. Let ν^β\widehat{\nu}_{\beta} be the empirical β\beta-quantile of Rτθ(1)(1),…,Rτθ(B)(B)R_{\tau_{\theta}^{(1)}}^{(1)},\ldots,R_{\tau_{\theta}^{(B)}}^{(B)}. The CVaR-PG gradient estimator is

g^PG(θ)=1β​B∑i=1B{Rτθ(i)(i)≤ν^β}(Rτθ(i)(i)−ν^β)∇θlogπθ(i)(τθ(i)).\widehat{g}_{\rm PG}(\theta)=\frac{1}{\beta B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\mathbf{1}\!\left\{R_{\tau_{\theta}^{(i)}}^{(i)}\leq\widehat{\nu}_{\beta}\right\}\left(R_{\tau_{\theta}^{(i)}}^{(i)}-\widehat{\nu}_{\beta}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}^{(i)}(\tau_{\theta}^{(i)}). (15)

The CVaR-PG estimator g^PG​(θ)\widehat{g}_{\rm PG}(\theta) in (15) has blindness to success: trajectories with sampled stopping rewards above ν^β\widehat{\nu}_{\beta} receive zero weight.

Methods for improving sample efficiency in CVaR policy optimization modify the gradient estimator, the policy, or the sampling procedure. Greenberg et al. [10] pair a soft-risk schedule with a cross-entropy environment sampler that requires controllable environment dynamics. Luo et al. [18] combine a risk-averse policy with a risk-neutral policy trained via Implicit Q-Learning [14]. Kim and Min [13] weight individual costs using an auxiliary tail-probability predictor. Mead et al. [20] compute policy gradients from capped trajectory returns and update the cap during training, subject to an externally supplied minimum cap. Luo and Delage [17] augment CVaR-PG with a quantile-gradient term computed by an auxiliary quantile critic.

4.2 The DIOS algorithm

For a fixed policy ϕθ\phi^{\theta} and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), the CVaR envelope (8) is maximized at ν=VaRβ​(Rτθ)\nu=\mathrm{VaR}_{\beta}(R_{\tau_{\theta}}). DIOS, presented in Algorithm 1, samples one stopping time on each trajectory according to the current policy. The reward quantile is then estimated from the batch of rewards obtained at the sampled stopping times. Let νk\nu_{k} and βk\beta_{k} denote the quantile estimate and tail level at iteration kk. With νk\nu_{k} held fixed, the policy update sums the terms −βk−1​(νk−Rt)+​∇θψtθ-\beta_{k}^{-1}(\nu_{k}-R_{t})^{+}\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta} over all stopping times on each trajectory. Thus a reward Rt<νkR_{t}<\nu_{k} can contribute even when the reward at the sampled stopping time exceeds νk\nu_{k}. Computing νk\nu_{k} directly from the batch removes the auxiliary critic.

Tail-level annealing gradually shifts training toward the target lower tail. The fractions ρw\rho_{w} and ρa\rho_{a} specify the warmup and annealing durations, respectively. During warmup, βk=1\beta_{k}=1 and νk\nu_{k} is the largest of the BB sampled stopping rewards. Since ∑t=0T∇θψtθ=0\sum_{t=0}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta}=0 and −(νk−Rt)+=min⁡{Rt,νk}−νk-(\nu_{k}-R_{t})^{+}=\min\{R_{t},\nu_{k}\}-\nu_{k}, the warmup gradient equals the pathwise gradient with rewards min⁡{Rt,νk}\min\{R_{t},\nu_{k}\}. Warmup therefore trains on rewards truncated at the batch maximum of sampled stopping rewards. After warmup, βk\beta_{k} decreases linearly to βtgt\beta_{\rm tgt} and remains at βtgt\beta_{\rm tgt} for the rest of training.

4.3 Finite-time convergence

We establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee for the DIOS update at a fixed tail level and bound the reward-quantile estimation error.

Fix β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). Define

Vβ​(θ):=CVaRβ​(Rτθ),Fθ​(x):=ℙ⁡(Rτθ≤x).V_{\beta}(\theta):=\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(R_{\tau_{\theta}}),\qquad F_{\theta}(x):=\mathbb{P}(R_{\tau_{\theta}}\leq x).
Assumption 4.1 (Convergence regime).

There exist a nonempty open convex domain U⊂ΘU\subset\Theta and numbers ν−>0\nu_{-}>0, f−>0f_{-}>0, δ0>0\delta_{0}>0, and LV>0L_{V}>0. Define

Θν−:={θ∈U:ν∗​(θ)≥ν−}.\Theta_{\nu_{-}}:=\{\theta\in U:\nu^{*}(\theta)\geq\nu_{-}\}.
  1. (a)

    For every θ∈Θν−\theta\in\Theta_{\nu_{-}} and u∈[0,δ0]u\in[0,\delta_{0}],

    Fθ​(ν∗​(θ)+u)≥β+f−​u,Fθ​(ν∗​(θ)−u)≤β−f−​u.F_{\theta}\bigl(\nu^{*}(\theta)+u\bigr)\geq\beta+f_{-}u,\qquad F_{\theta}\bigl(\nu^{*}(\theta)-u\bigr)\leq\beta-f_{-}u.
  2. (b)

    The function VβV_{\beta} is differentiable on UU, and ∇Vβ\nabla V_{\beta} is LVL_{V}-Lipschitz on UU.

For each integer batch size B≥1B\geq 1, fix an integer mBm_{B} satisfying

1≤mB≤B,|mB−β​B|≤1.1\leq m_{B}\leq B,\qquad|m_{B}-\beta B|\leq 1. (16)

Let ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k} be the sigma-field generated by θ0\theta_{0} and all state trajectories and stopping draws before iteration kk. Conditional on ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k}, sample BB independent copies of (St)t=0T(S_{t})_{t=0}^{T}. For each trajectory ii, draw τθk(i)\tau_{\theta_{k}}^{(i)} with probabilities (ψtθk,(i))t=0T(\psi_{t}^{\theta_{k},(i)})_{t=0}^{T}, independently across ii conditional on the state trajectories. Let νk\nu_{k} be the mBm_{B}-th smallest reward among Rτθk(i)(i)R_{\tau_{\theta_{k}}^{(i)}}^{(i)}, i=1,…,Bi=1,\ldots,B. For a constant step size η>0\eta>0, define

g^k(ν):=−1β​B∑i=1B∑t=0T(ν−Rt(i))+∇θψtθ,(i)|θ=θk,θk+1=θk+ηg^k(νk).\widehat{g}_{k}(\nu):=-\frac{1}{\beta B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{t=0}^{T}(\nu-R_{t}^{(i)})^{+}\left.\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta,(i)}\right|_{\theta=\theta_{k}},\qquad\theta_{k+1}=\theta_{k}+\eta\widehat{g}_{k}(\nu_{k}). (17)

Assumption 4.1(b) gives [9]

Vβ​(θ′)≥Vβ​(θ)+⟨∇Vβ​(θ),θ′−θ⟩−LV2​‖θ′−θ‖2,θ,θ′∈U.V_{\beta}(\theta^{\prime})\geq V_{\beta}(\theta)+\langle\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta),\theta^{\prime}-\theta\rangle-\tfrac{L_{V}}{2}\|\theta^{\prime}-\theta\|^{2},\qquad\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in U.
Theorem 4.2 (Finite-time convergence).

Under Assumptions 3.5, 3.8, and 4.1, there exist an integer B0≥1B_{0}\geq 1 and constants Cν>0C_{\nu}>0 and Cg≥0C_{g}\geq 0, depending only on β\beta, TT, MM, CψC_{\psi}, f−f_{-}, and δ0\delta_{0}. Let K,BK,B be integers with K≥1K\geq 1 and B≥B0B\geq B_{0}, and let 0<η≤1/LV0<\eta\leq 1/L_{V}. Suppose (θk)k=0K(\theta_{k})_{k=0}^{K} satisfies (17) and θk∈Θν−\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{\nu_{-}} almost surely for 0≤k≤K0\leq k\leq K. Define

D0:=supϑ∈ΘVβ​(ϑ)−𝔼⁡[Vβ​(θ0)].D_{0}:=\sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta}V_{\beta}(\vartheta)-\mathbb{E}[V_{\beta}(\theta_{0})].

Then the following bounds hold.

  1. (a)

    The reward-quantile estimates νk\nu_{k} satisfy

    max0≤k<K⁡𝔼⁡[(νk−ν∗​(θk))2]≤CνB.\max_{0\leq k<K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\nu_{k}-\nu^{*}(\theta_{k}))^{2}\right]\leq\frac{C_{\nu}}{B}. (18)
  2. (b)

    The average expected squared gradient satisfies

    1K​∑k=0K−1𝔼⁡[‖∇Vβ​(θk)‖2]≤2​D0η​K+CgB.\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta_{k})\|^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2D_{0}}{\eta K}+\frac{C_{g}}{B}. (19)

Consequently,

min0≤k<K⁡𝔼⁡[‖∇Vβ​(θk)‖2+(νk−ν∗​(θk))2]≤2​D0η​K+Cg+CνB.\min_{0\leq k<K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta_{k})\|^{2}+(\nu_{k}-\nu^{*}(\theta_{k}))^{2}\right]\leq\frac{2D_{0}}{\eta K}+\frac{C_{g}+C_{\nu}}{B}. (20)

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, integers K≥1K\geq 1 and B≥B0B\geq B_{0} can be chosen so that

min0≤k<K⁡𝔼⁡[‖∇Vβ​(θk)‖2+(νk−ν∗​(θk))2]≤ϵ,\min_{0\leq k<K}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta_{k})\|^{2}+(\nu_{k}-\nu^{*}(\theta_{k}))^{2}\right]\leq\epsilon,

provided the corresponding iterates satisfy θk∈Θν−\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{\nu_{-}} almost surely. For fixed β\beta and η\eta and sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the choices satisfy K=O⁡(ϵ−1)K=O(\epsilon^{-1}) and B=O⁡(ϵ−1)B=O(\epsilon^{-1}), giving K​B=O⁡(ϵ−2)KB=O(\epsilon^{-2}) sampled trajectories.

Remark 4.3.

Theorem 4.2 applies when quantile estimation and the policy update use the same batch. Since νk\nu_{k} depends on the sampled trajectories, g^k​(νk)\widehat{g}_{k}(\nu_{k}) need not be conditionally unbiased for ∇Vβ​(θk)\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta_{k}) given ℋk\mathcal{H}_{k}. The proof in Appendix B establishes

𝔼⁡[‖g^k​(νk)−∇Vβ​(θk)‖2∣ℋk]≤Cg/B\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{g}_{k}(\nu_{k})-\nabla V_{\beta}(\theta_{k})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{k}\right]\leq C_{g}/B

by bounding the sampling error at ν∗​(θk)\nu^{*}(\theta_{k}) and the error from replacing ν∗​(θk)\nu^{*}(\theta_{k}) with νk\nu_{k}.

5 Empirical validation

We validate DIOS on Bermudan max-call options against four CVaR baselines: CVaR-PG [25], MIX [18], RET-CAP [20], and CVaR-VaR [17]. Appendix D.1 reports additional results for PCVaR-PG [13]. The setup uses volatility σ=0.20\sigma=0.20, d∈{20,50,100,200}d\in\{20,50,100,200\} underlying assets, initial price s0∈{90,100,110}s_{0}\in\{90,100,110\}, 1010 candidate stopping times t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T with T=9T=9, and CVaR level β=0.2\beta=0.2, yielding 12 configurations. An asymmetric-volatility variant reported in Appendix E.1 contributes 12 more, for 24 in total. We estimate CVaR0.2 by averaging the lowest 20%20\% of evaluation rewards. Let τ¯∈[0,T]\bar{\tau}\in[0,T] denote the mean stopping time on the evaluation set. For each configuration, the top row of Table 1 reports the mean and standard deviation of CVaR0.2 over ten training seeds. The bottom row reports training time in seconds, including periodic evaluation, and the fraction of seeds with τ¯<0.5\bar{\tau}<0.5, which we classify as collapsed. Bold entries mark the highest mean CVaR and shortest training time. Implementation details are in Appendix C.

DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time in all 24 symmetric and asymmetric configurations. CVaR-PG and MIX have large standard deviations and collapsed seeds, with collapse rates of 3/103/10 and 5/105/10, respectively, at symmetric (d,s0)=(20,110)(d,s_{0})=(20,110). CVaR-VaR takes roughly 44–55 times as long as DIOS, while MIX and RET-CAP take roughly twice as long. Appendix D.5 compares CVaR-VaR with a variant that replaces the quantile critic by a batch mean and changes the tradeoff-weight schedule. For RET-CAP, we compute the minimum cap q∗q^{*} by averaging empirical β\beta-quantiles of DIOS evaluation rewards over ten seeds. Appendix D.2 specifies the calculation and Appendix E.1 reports the asymmetric results.

The mean advantage over CVaR-VaR is small in some configurations. At symmetric (d,s0)=(200,110)(d,s_{0})=(200,110), mean CVaR is 89.37889.378 for DIOS and 89.37589.375 for CVaR-VaR. Two-sided paired tt-tests over ten training seeds give p<0.05p<0.05 against CVaR-VaR in 5 of the 24 configurations. The pp-values are not adjusted for testing multiple configurations. Appendix C gives the paired mean differences and pp-values.

Additional experiments.

Appendix F compares raw batch quantile estimates with exponential moving average (EMA) estimates within DIOS at β=0.1\beta=0.1 and 0.050.05. DIOS with EMA has the highest mean CVaR among the tested methods in all 12 configurations at each tail level. Paired tt-tests give p<0.05p<0.05 against CVaR-VaR in 6/12 configurations at β=0.1\beta=0.1 and 12/12 at β=0.05\beta=0.05, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons. Appendix G reports house-selling experiments, where DIOS has the highest mean CVaR in 23/24 configurations. Appendix H compares CVaR, parameter counts, and training times for DIOS encoder widths 32–256.

6 Conclusion

We developed a framework and algorithm for CVaR deep optimal stopping. The properties (S1)–(S3) yield Markov optimality without state augmentation and a pathwise gradient formula. Theorem 3.10 contrasts bounded pathwise second moments with score-function divergence under the stated conditions. DIOS combines a per-time-step soft penalty, tail-level annealing, and direct batch quantile estimation. We establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee at a fixed tail level. DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time across the 24 max-call configurations.

Limitations and future work.

Theorem 4.2 bounds expected squared gradients and squared quantile errors at fixed β\beta under Assumptions 3.5, 3.8, and 4.1, with θk∈Θν−\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{\nu_{-}} throughout the analyzed updates. The theorem does not establish parameter convergence or global optimality. The score-function and pathwise estimators can each vanish under the sigmoid conditions in Appendix B. Appendix A explains why ReLU, unbounded inputs, training-mode BatchNorm, and reward atoms prevent automatic verification of the assumptions. Extending the convergence analysis to Adam, clipping, training-mode BatchNorm, annealing, and EMA remains open. At β=1\beta=1, unbounded rewards can preclude a finite maximizing ν\nu in (8).

The annealing ablation also changes the quantile rank, and the critic ablation also changes the tradeoff-weight schedule. Recorded training times come from different sessions, sometimes on shared GPUs, and exclude training and evaluation of policies used to set RET-CAP’s minimum cap. RET-CAP CVaR values and times use different settings, as specified in Table 1. The experiments cover max-call options, house selling, and encoder widths 32–256. Further work includes larger architectures, action-dependent dynamics, and convergence for other optimized certainty equivalent objectives. Medical and control applications require validation of tail estimates to limit human and financial costs.

Appendix A Assumptions in the experimental domains

We verify the payoff-moment assumptions and examine the additional policy and convergence conditions in the experimental domains.

A.1 Model and payoff moments

Max-call rewards.

Let StjS_{t}^{j} denote the price of asset j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}, with S0j=s0S_{0}^{j}=s_{0}. Asset prices follow independent geometric Brownian motions under the risk-neutral measure, with drift r−δr-\delta and volatility σj\sigma_{j}. Prices are sampled at t=0,…,T=9t=0,\ldots,T=9 with time step Δ​t=1/3\Delta t=1/3 year. Let Kstrike=100K_{\rm strike}=100 and define

Rt:=e−r​t​Δ​t​(max1≤j≤d⁡Stj−Kstrike)+.R_{t}:=e^{-rt\Delta t}\left(\max_{1\leq j\leq d}S_{t}^{j}-K_{\rm strike}\right)^{+}.

The experiments use r=0.05r=0.05, δ=0.10\delta=0.10, d∈{20,50,100,200}d\in\{20,50,100,200\}, and s0∈{90,100,110}s_{0}\in\{90,100,110\}. The symmetric domain has σj=0.20\sigma_{j}=0.20. The asymmetric domain has σj=0.10+j/(2​d)\sigma_{j}=0.10+j/(2d). Every asset price has finite moments of all orders. Since

0≤Rt≤∑j=1dStj,Rt2≤∑j=1d(Stj)2,0\leq R_{t}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}S_{t}^{j},\qquad R_{t}^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}(S_{t}^{j})^{2},

Assumptions 2.1 and 3.8 hold in both domains, with M=max0≤t≤T⁡‖Rt‖L2​(P)<∞M=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\|R_{t}\|_{L^{2}(P)}<\infty.

House-selling rewards.

Let Xj>0X_{j}>0 be the offer at decision j∈{1,…,9}j\in\{1,\ldots,9\} and let c>0c>0 be the cost per decision. Accepting at jj gives Xj−c​jX_{j}-cj, which can be negative. Adding 9​c9c to the reward at every decision makes the rewards nonnegative. For each fixed policy, CVaR and VaR increase by 9​c9c. Replacing RtR_{t} by Rt+9​cR_{t}+9c and ν\nu by ν+9​c\nu+9c leaves (ν−Rt)+(\nu-R_{t})^{+} and the pathwise gradient unchanged. The tables retain the original reward units. Lognormal offers and the tested Pareto shapes a>2a>2 have finite second moments.

A.2 Policy regularity

Sigmoid output.

For a finite logit ztθ​(St)z_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t}), the probability ϕtθ​(St)=(1+e−ztθ​(St))−1\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t})=(1+e^{-z_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t})})^{-1} lies in (0,1)(0,1) for t<Tt<T. Forced terminal stopping gives ϕTθ​(ST)=1\phi_{T}^{\theta}(S_{T})=1 and ∇θϕTθ​(ST)=0\nabla_{\theta}\phi_{T}^{\theta}(S_{T})=0. A sigmoid output does not by itself imply the uniform derivative bound in Assumption 3.5. For example, ϕθ​(s)=(1+e−θ​s)−1\phi^{\theta}(s)=(1+e^{-\theta s})^{-1} has derivative s/4s/4 at θ=0\theta=0, which is unbounded as s→∞s\to\infty.

Derivatives of stopping probabilities.

Suppose ‖∇θϕtθ​(St)‖≤G\|\nabla_{\theta}\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t})\|\leq G uniformly in tt and θ\theta, as required by Assumption 3.5. The derivative formula in Remark 3.7 contains probability factors in [0,1][0,1]. The triangle inequality therefore gives

‖∇θψtθ‖≤G⁡(1+t)≤G⁡(T+1).\|\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta}\|\leq G(1+t)\leq G(T+1). (21)

Thus Cψ=G⁡(T+1)C_{\psi}=G(T+1) is a valid choice in Assumption 3.5. For a bound independent of TT, suppose additionally that ϕsθ​(Ss)≥ϕ−\phi_{s}^{\theta}(S_{s})\geq\phi_{-} for every s<Ts<T and θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta on an event of probability one, where ϕ−∈(0,1)\phi_{-}\in(0,1). For 1≤t≤T1\leq t\leq T,

‖∇θψtθ‖≤G​(1−ϕ−)t+t​G​(1−ϕ−)t−1.\|\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{t}^{\theta}\|\leq G(1-\phi_{-})^{t}+tG(1-\phi_{-})^{t-1}.

At t=0t=0, ‖∇θψ0θ‖≤G\|\nabla_{\theta}\psi_{0}^{\theta}\|\leq G. Consequently, a valid choice is

Cψ=G​max⁡{1,supm∈{1,2,…}[(1−ϕ−)m+m​(1−ϕ−)m−1]}<∞.C_{\psi}=G\max\left\{1,\sup_{m\in\{1,2,\ldots\}}\bigl[(1-\phi_{-})^{m}+m(1-\phi_{-})^{m-1}\bigr]\right\}<\infty.

Finiteness follows from m​(1−ϕ−)m−1→0m(1-\phi_{-})^{m-1}\to 0. For fixed GG and ϕ−\phi_{-}, the bound CψC_{\psi} is independent of TT.

Training implementation.

The network in Appendix C uses ReLU and BatchNorm. ReLU is not differentiable at zero, and the lognormal inputs are unbounded. During training, BatchNorm statistics use all B⁡(T+1)B(T+1) state-time pairs, so a probability at time tt can depend on future states and other trajectories. The training computation therefore differs from the pointwise policy ϕtθ​(St)\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t}) assumed in the analysis. Evaluation uses fixed running statistics. The architecture alone does not establish Assumption 3.5.

A.3 Convergence assumptions and training diagnostics

Terminal-stop benchmark.

For nonnegative RTR_{T}, CVaRβ​(RT)>0\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(R_{T})>0 if and only if P⁡(RT=0)<βP(R_{T}=0)<\beta. Let Φ\Phi denote the standard normal CDF. In the symmetric domain, T​Δ​t=3T\Delta t=3 and r−δ−σ2/2=−0.07r-\delta-\sigma^{2}/2=-0.07, giving

P⁡(RT=0)=Φ​(log⁡(Kstrike/s0)+0.210.2​3)d.P(R_{T}=0)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log(K_{\rm strike}/s_{0})+0.21}{0.2\sqrt{3}}\right)^{d}.

The largest probability on the tested grid occurs at (d,s0)=(20,90)(d,s_{0})=(20,90) and is below 0.01830.0183. In the asymmetric domain,

P⁡(RT=0)=∏j=1dΦ⁡(log⁡(Kstrike/s0)−3​(r−δ−σj2/2)σj​3).P(R_{T}=0)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log(K_{\rm strike}/s_{0})-3(r-\delta-\sigma_{j}^{2}/2)}{\sigma_{j}\sqrt{3}}\right).

The largest probability again occurs at (d,s0)=(20,90)(d,s_{0})=(20,90) and is below 0.008610.00861. Hence stopping at TT gives positive CVaR at every tested target tail level in both domains.

Conditions along the iterates.

The terminal-stop calculation establishes a positive-CVaR benchmark. Theorem 4.2 additionally requires the CDF bounds in Assumption 4.1(a), a differentiable VβV_{\beta} with an LVL_{V}-Lipschitz gradient on UU, and ν∗​(θk)≥ν−\nu^{*}(\theta_{k})\geq\nu_{-} throughout the analyzed updates. Max-call rewards have an atom at zero, so the CDF bounds cannot be inferred from the continuous asset-price distributions. During the fixed-tail phase, the recorded batch estimate νk\nu_{k} is zero in 6 of 180,000 symmetric-domain updates and 2 of 180,000 asymmetric-domain updates. Counts of zero νk\nu_{k} do not verify ν∗​(θk)≥ν−\nu^{*}(\theta_{k})\geq\nu_{-}.

Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

For every X∈L1​(P)X\in L^{1}(P), the representation (8) gives

CVaRβ​(X)=supν∈ℝF⁡(ν,X)withF⁡(ν,X):=ν+1β​𝔼​[−(ν−X)+],\mathrm{CVaR}_{\beta}(X)\;=\;\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}F(\nu,X)\quad\text{with}\quad F(\nu,X)\;:=\;\nu+\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[-(\nu-X)^{+}\right],

where the supremum is attained at ν=VaRβ​(X)\nu=\mathrm{VaR}_{\beta}(X). Assumption 2.1 gives Rτ∈L1​(P)R_{\tau}\in L^{1}(P) for every τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, so we may set X=RτX=R_{\tau}.

By the commutativity of iterated suprema,

Vβ∗=supτ∈𝒯supν∈ℝF⁡(ν,Rτ)=supν∈ℝΦ⁡(ν),V^{*}_{\beta}\;=\;\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}F(\nu,R_{\tau})\;=\;\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}\Phi(\nu),

where

Φ⁡(ν):=supτ∈𝒯fτ​(ν),fτ​(ν):=ν+1β​𝔼​[−(ν−Rτ)+].\Phi(\nu)\;:=\;\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}f_{\tau}(\nu),\qquad f_{\tau}(\nu)\;:=\;\nu+\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\mathbb{E}[-(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}].

Equation (10) follows.

For each x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, ν↦−(ν−x)+\nu\mapsto-(\nu-x)^{+} is 11-Lipschitz:

|−(ν1−x)++(ν2−x)+|≤|ν1−ν2|.\bigl|-(\nu_{1}-x)^{+}+(\nu_{2}-x)^{+}\bigr|\;\leq\;|\nu_{1}-\nu_{2}|.

Hence ν↦𝔼⁡[−(ν−Rτ)+]\nu\mapsto\mathbb{E}[-(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}] is 11-Lipschitz for every τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, and fτf_{\tau} is (1+1/β)(1+1/\beta)-Lipschitz. Since −(ν−x)+≤0-(\nu-x)^{+}\leq 0, fτ​(ν)≤νf_{\tau}(\nu)\leq\nu, so Φ⁡(ν)≤ν<∞\Phi(\nu)\leq\nu<\infty for every ν∈ℝ\nu\in\mathbb{R}. A pointwise-finite supremum of LL-Lipschitz functions is again LL-Lipschitz, so Φ\Phi is (1+1/β)(1+1/\beta)-Lipschitz.

For ν≤0\nu\leq 0, Rτ≥0R_{\tau}\geq 0 (since each gtg_{t} takes values in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}) gives (ν−Rτ)+=0(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}=0, hence 𝔼⁡[−(ν−Rτ)+]=0\mathbb{E}[-(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}]=0 for every τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} and

Φ⁡(ν)=ν(ν≤0).\Phi(\nu)\;=\;\nu\qquad(\nu\leq 0).

In particular Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(0)=0, and Φ⁡(ν)→−∞\Phi(\nu)\to-\infty as ν→−∞\nu\to-\infty.

The bound −(ν−Rτ)+≤−(ν−Rτ)-(\nu-R_{\tau})^{+}\leq-(\nu-R_{\tau}) is pointwise, so

Φ⁡(ν)≤ν+1β​(−ν+supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[Rτ])=(1−1/β)​ν+1β​supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[Rτ].\Phi(\nu)\;\leq\;\nu+\tfrac{1}{\beta}\!\left(-\nu+\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[R_{\tau}]\right)\;=\;(1-1/\beta)\,\nu\;+\;\tfrac{1}{\beta}\,\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[R_{\tau}].

Since Rt≥0R_{t}\geq 0, Rτ=∑t=0TRt𝟏{τ=t}≤∑t=0TRtR_{\tau}=\sum_{t=0}^{T}R_{t}\mathbf{1}\{\tau=t\}\leq\sum_{t=0}^{T}R_{t}, hence

supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[Rτ]≤∑t=0T𝔼⁡[Rt]=:C<∞\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[R_{\tau}]\;\leq\;\sum_{t=0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[R_{t}]\;=:\;C\;<\;\infty

by Assumption 2.1. Hence Φ⁡(ν)≤(1−1/β)​ν+C/β\Phi(\nu)\leq(1-1/\beta)\,\nu+C/\beta, and since 1−1/β<01-1/\beta<0, Φ⁡(ν)→−∞\Phi(\nu)\to-\infty as ν→+∞\nu\to+\infty.

Φ\Phi is continuous and Φ⁡(ν)→−∞\Phi(\nu)\to-\infty as |ν|→∞|\nu|\to\infty, so there is K>0K>0 with Φ⁡(ν)<0\Phi(\nu)<0 for |ν|>K|\nu|>K. Proof.

By Proposition 3.1, there exists ν∗∈ℝ\nu^{*}\in\mathbb{R} attaining the outer supremum in (10). Define htν∗:=−(ν∗−Rt)+h^{\nu^{*}}_{t}:=-(\nu^{*}-R_{t})^{+} and the Snell envelope

VTν∗:=hTν∗,Vtν∗:=max(htν∗,𝔼[Vt+1ν∗∣ℱt])(t<T).V^{\nu^{*}}_{T}\;:=\;h^{\nu^{*}}_{T},\qquad V^{\nu^{*}}_{t}\;:=\;\max\bigl(h^{\nu^{*}}_{t},\ \mathbb{E}[V^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\bigr)\quad(t<T).

By Shiryaev [24], τν∗:=inf{t≥0:Vtν∗=htν∗}\tau^{\nu^{*}}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:V^{\nu^{*}}_{t}=h^{\nu^{*}}_{t}\} attains supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[hτν∗]\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[h^{\nu^{*}}_{\tau}].

It suffices to find Borel sets D0,…,DT⊆ℝdD_{0},\dots,D_{T}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with DT=ℝdD_{T}=\mathbb{R}^{d} and

τν∗=inf{t≥0:St∈Dt}P​-a.s.\tau^{\nu^{*}}\;=\;\inf\{t\geq 0:S_{t}\in D_{t}\}\quad P\text{-a.s.}

Define the Borel function h~tν∗:ℝd→ℝ\tilde{h}^{\nu^{*}}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} by h~tν∗​(s):=−(ν∗−gt​(s))+\tilde{h}^{\nu^{*}}_{t}(s):=-(\nu^{*}-g_{t}(s))^{+}. By (S1), htν∗=h~tν∗​(St)h^{\nu^{*}}_{t}=\tilde{h}^{\nu^{*}}_{t}(S_{t}).

Backward induction gives Borel functions vtν∗:ℝd→ℝv^{\nu^{*}}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} with vtν∗​(St)∈L1​(P)v^{\nu^{*}}_{t}(S_{t})\in L^{1}(P) satisfying

Vtν∗=vtν∗​(St)P​-a.s.V^{\nu^{*}}_{t}\;=\;v^{\nu^{*}}_{t}(S_{t})\quad P\text{-a.s.}

Suppose Vt+1ν∗=vt+1ν∗​(St+1)V^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}=v^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}(S_{t+1}) PP-a.s. for some Borel vt+1ν∗v^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1} with vt+1ν∗​(St+1)∈L1​(P)v^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\in L^{1}(P). Since (St)t=0T(S_{t})_{t=0}^{T} is Markov,

𝔼⁡[Vt+1ν∗∣ℱt]=𝔼⁡[vt+1ν∗​(St+1)∣St].\mathbb{E}[V^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}[v^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\mid S_{t}].

By Doob-Dynkin, there is a Borel qtν∗:ℝd→ℝq^{\nu^{*}}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} with 𝔼⁡[vt+1ν∗​(St+1)∣St]=qtν∗​(St)\mathbb{E}[v^{\nu^{*}}_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\mid S_{t}]=q^{\nu^{*}}_{t}(S_{t}) PP-a.s. Define

combined with Assumption 2.1 and the conditional Jensen inequality.

Appendix C Implementation details for the symmetric Bermudan max-call domain

We follow the LunarLander protocol of Luo and Delage [17] with the following changes. (i) The discount γ=1\gamma=1 since the max-call payoff e−r​t​Δ​t​(maxj⁡Stj−Kstrike)+e^{-rt\Delta t}(\max_{j}S_{t}^{j}-K_{\rm strike})^{+} already discounts through the e−r​t​Δ​te^{-rt\Delta t} factor (with Δ​t=1/3\Delta t=1/3 year). (ii) The feature vector is (St/100,t/T,Rt)(S_{t}/100,\,t/T,\,R_{t}), providing the time index and the immediate payoff suited to optimal stopping. (iii) BatchNorm is applied to the encoder. (iv) The policy logit at t=Tt=T is set to +20+20. (v) Policy gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 1.01.0. (vi) The IQL batch size of MIX scales linearly with horizon TT from the LunarLander value in Luo et al. [18]: 2×1052\times 10^{5} transitions per update at T=500T=500 becomes 3,6003{,}600 at T=9T=9. The IQL replay buffer holds 10610^{6} transitions. Tables 2, 3, and 4 specify the domain components, training protocol, and per-method hyperparameters, respectively.

Policy and quantile implementation.

The encoder has two Linear–BatchNorm–ReLU blocks of width 128, followed by a 128→64→1128\to 64\to 1 policy head with ReLU and sigmoid output. During training, BatchNorm computes statistics across the B⁡(T+1)B(T+1) sampled state-time pairs. Dropout is disabled. Rewards are divided by the standard deviation of the B⁡(T+1)B(T+1) payoffs in the first batch, and the normalization scale is held fixed throughout training. The implementation estimates the reward quantile using the order statistic of rank max⁡{1,⌊βk​B⌋}\max\{1,\lfloor\beta_{k}B\rfloor\} from the sampled stopping rewards. Floating-point schedule arithmetic gives hold-phase ranks 3,1,13,1,1 at target levels 0.2,0.1,0.050.2,0.1,0.05 with B=20B=20. Two annealing updates at target 0.20.2 use ranks 77 and 55 instead of 88 and 66. With annealing disabled, the separate branch uses rank 44 at 0.20.2. The loss is the stop-gradient surrogate in Algorithm 1, with log⁡ψt\log\psi_{t} computed from log-sigmoid sums and νk\nu_{k} held fixed during differentiation.

Compute.

Experiments ran on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs, with each job assigned to one GPU. Some jobs shared a GPU. Training times include trajectory simulation, gradient updates, logging, and six periodic evaluations of 5,0005{,}000 paths. Model creation and the final 20,00020{,}000-path evaluation are excluded. RET-CAP times also exclude training and evaluation of the policies used to set the minimum cap. The RET-CAP CVaR values come from reruns with recomputed minimum caps and retuned hyperparameters, while the tables retain the training times measured with the earlier minimum caps and hyperparameters.

Evaluation.

Each final policy is evaluated on 20,00020{,}000 paths with seed 10000+s10000+s for training seed s∈{0,…,9}s\in\{0,\ldots,9\}. Methods share evaluation paths for each seed. Evaluation uses BatchNorm running statistics and stops at the first tt with ϕtθ​(St)>0.5\phi_{t}^{\theta}(S_{t})>0.5. At β=0.2\beta=0.2, CVaR is the mean of exactly the lowest 4,0004{,}000 rewards. Means and population standard deviations are over ten training seeds.

Paired comparisons.

Table 5 reports two-sided paired tt and exact Wilcoxon tests over training seeds, using shared evaluation paths per seed and no multiple-comparison correction. DIOS has a higher mean CVaR than CVaR-VaR in all 24 max-call configurations, with paired tt-test p<0.05p<0.05 against CVaR-VaR in 2 symmetric and 3 asymmetric configurations.

Appendix D Additional baseline experiments on the symmetric Bermudan max-call domain

D.1 PCVaR-PG

Table 6 reports PCVaR-PG [13] on all twelve symmetric configurations. At s0=110s_{0}=110, all ten seeds stop immediately and receive reward 1010. At s0∈{90,100}s_{0}\in\{90,100\}, the mean stopping time ranges from 1.01.0 to 3.43.4.

D.2 RET-CAP minimum cap and the choice of anchor

RET-CAP updates a return cap during training and constrains the cap to be at least an externally supplied value q∗q^{*} [20]. In the max-call experiments, we compute the empirical β\beta-quantile of the evaluation rewards for each trained DIOS policy. We average the quantiles over ten seeds and round to three decimal places to obtain q∗q^{*}. The tables label the DIOS-derived minimum cap “cap-anchor”. Appendix D.3 compares the DIOS-derived minimum cap with a minimum cap computed from separately trained risk-neutral policies. The choice of an evaluation VaR as the minimum cap is part of our experimental protocol.

D.3 RET-CAP with risk-neutral anchor

We additionally set the RET-CAP minimum cap from the evaluation quantiles of separately trained risk-neutral (RN) policies on the symmetric domain. Table 7 compares the DIOS-derived and risk-neutral minimum caps, with hyperparameters selected separately for each choice. The asymmetric counterpart is reported in Appendix E.3.

D.4 DIOS ablations

We compare variants of two design choices in DIOS: the soft-penalty CVaR objective and the β\beta-anneal schedule.

Risk-neutral baseline.

We train the same DIOS architecture under the risk-neutral expectation JRN​(θ)=𝔼⁡[∑tψtθ​Rt]J_{\rm RN}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\psi_{t}^{\theta}R_{t}], replacing the soft-penalty objective with expected reward and omitting quantile estimation. We evaluate the risk-neutral policy and DIOS using CVaR0.2 on the same evaluation paths for each seed. Table 8 reports CVaR0.2 for the risk-neutral policy and DIOS, together with the difference, risk-neutral minus DIOS.

β\beta-anneal ablation.

We disable both the warmup and anneal phases, setting ρw=ρa=0\rho_{w}=\rho_{a}=0 so that βk=βtgt=0.2\beta_{k}=\beta_{\rm tgt}=0.2 from iteration k=0k=0. Table 9 reports the comparison on the symmetric domain. Without the schedule, all ten seeds collapse at (d,s0)=(20,110)(d,s_{0})=(20,110), and two of ten seeds collapse in each configuration with d∈{100,200}d\in\{100,200\}. The full-schedule and no-schedule runs use hold-phase quantile ranks three and four, respectively.

D.5 CVaR-VaR critic ablation

CVaR-VaR [17] uses a state-dependent quantile critic to track quantile levels and compute multi-step advantages for the VaR-gradient term. Our implementation uses a separate 128128-unit MLP trained by multi-step quantile regression at each iteration, adding a critic forward pass and optimizer step to each policy update.

The no-critic variant replaces the critic prediction at every state with the preceding batch’s mean stopping reward after normalization. At the first update, the baseline is the mean unnormalized terminal payoff in the batch. The no-critic variant also holds the tradeoff weight ω\omega at 0.50.5 for the first 40% of training and then decreases ω\omega linearly to zero. The main CVaR-VaR baseline uses ω=0.5\omega=0.5 throughout.

In every configuration in Table 10, the no-critic variant has shorter recorded training time and lower mean CVaR than the main CVaR-VaR baseline.

Appendix F Smaller tail levels and quantile smoothing

Table 18 reports the symmetric max-call grid at β=0.1\beta=0.1 and 0.050.05. Raw DIOS uses the current batch order statistic as the quantile estimate. For DIOS with an exponential moving average (EMA), denoted ν\nu-EMA, let ν^k\widehat{\nu}_{k} be the batch order statistic and define

ν0=ν^0,νk=(1−α)νk−1+αν^k(k≥1).\nu_{0}=\widehat{\nu}_{0},\qquad\nu_{k}=(1-\alpha)\nu_{k-1}+\alpha\widehat{\nu}_{k}\quad(k\geq 1).

The smoothing is applied from the beginning of training, including warmup and annealing. The weight α\alpha multiplies the new batch statistic. We select α=0.9\alpha=0.9 at β=0.1\beta=0.1 on (d,s0)=(200,100)(d,s_{0})=(200,100) and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 at β=0.05\beta=0.05 on (d,s0)=(20,90)(d,s_{0})=(20,90), using seeds 0–2. The final comparison uses ten seeds. DIOS retains learning rate 7×10−57\times 10^{-5}. CVaR-VaR uses learning rate 10−410^{-4}, value multiplier one, and fixed tradeoff weight ω=0.5\omega=0.5. CVaR-PG uses learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}.

DIOS with EMA exceeds CVaR-VaR and CVaR-PG in mean CVaR in all 12 configurations at each tail level. Two-sided paired tt-tests over ten seeds give p<0.05p<0.05 against CVaR-VaR in 6/12 configurations at β=0.1\beta=0.1 and 12/12 at β=0.05\beta=0.05. The pp-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Raw DIOS has a higher mean CVaR than CVaR-VaR and CVaR-PG in 1 of 12 configurations at β=0.1\beta=0.1 and 8 of 12 configurations at β=0.05\beta=0.05. The improvement from smoothing is observed with batch size B=20B=20.

Appendix G House selling

Offers X1,…,X9X_{1},\ldots,X_{9} arrive independently with mean 50. The seller observes one offer at each decision point j=1,…,9j=1,\ldots,9, can accept only the current offer, and must accept by j=9j=9. Accepting at jj gives Xj−c​jX_{j}-cj, so the first observed offer already incurs cost cc. There is no stopping decision before the first offer. Relabeling the offer times as t=0,…,8t=0,\ldots,8 gives the time convention of Section 2. The policy observes the normalized current offer, time, and immediate payoff.

The lognormal grid uses log⁡Xj∼N⁡(log⁡50−σ2/2,σ2)\log X_{j}\sim N(\log 50-\sigma^{2}/2,\sigma^{2}) with σ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\sigma\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}. The Pareto grid uses shape a∈{6,4,3,2.5}a\in\{6,4,3,2.5\} and scale 50​(a−1)/a50(a-1)/a. Each family is crossed with c∈{1,2,3}c\in\{1,2,3\}, giving 24 cells. Finite second moments hold in both families. Negative rewards are possible in the lognormal grid, as discussed in Appendix A.

For every method, we select the policy learning rate from the sweep set in Appendix C. Selection uses (σ,c)=(0.5,2)(\sigma,c)=(0.5,2) for lognormal offers and (a,c)=(3,2)(a,c)=(3,2) for Pareto offers. Selection and final experiments use seeds 0–9. Other settings follow the max-call protocol. RET-CAP uses the seed-averaged DIOS evaluation VaR, rounded to six decimals, as the minimum cap, and the selected RET-CAP policy learning rates are 10−410^{-4} for lognormal offers and 7×10−57\times 10^{-5} for Pareto offers. Tables 19 and 20 report the complete results.

RET-CAP has the largest mean only for (σ,c)=(0.9,2)(\sigma,c)=(0.9,2), exceeding DIOS by approximately 0.0040.004, with paired tt-test p=0.99p=0.99. An alternative anchor from a policy trained with βk≡1\beta_{k}\equiv 1 gives RET-CAP 41.155±0.64941.155\pm 0.649 at (σ,c)=(0.9,2)(\sigma,c)=(0.9,2), compared with DIOS 41.729±0.97441.729\pm 0.974. The policy used to compute the house-selling alternative minimum cap is trained at βk=1\beta_{k}=1 with rewards truncated at the batch maximum of sampled stopping rewards. The max-call risk-neutral policies instead maximize expected payoff directly.

Appendix I An optimized certainty equivalent example

For a nondecreasing concave utility uu, define the optimized certainty equivalent [5] by OCEu⁡(X):=supν{ν+𝔼⁡[u⁡(X−ν)]}\operatorname{OCE}_{u}(X):=\sup_{\nu}\{\nu+\mathbb{E}[u(X-\nu)]\}. If u⁡(Rt−ν)u(R_{t}-\nu) is integrable for every tt and every fixed ν\nu, exchanging the two suprema as in Proposition 3.1 gives

supτ∈𝒯OCEu⁡(Rτ)=supν∈ℝ{ν+supτ∈𝒯𝔼⁡[u⁡(Rτ−ν)]}.\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\operatorname{OCE}_{u}(R_{\tau})=\sup_{\nu\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\nu+\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbb{E}[u(R_{\tau}-\nu)]\right\}.

For fixed ν\nu, the inner optimization is an expected-reward stopping problem with reward u⁡(Rt−ν)u(R_{t}-\nu). The outer optimization selects ν\nu. For each fixed ν\nu, the Snell envelope gives an optimizer of the inner problem. If the outer supremum is attained at ν∗\nu^{*}, a stopping time that optimizes the inner problem at ν∗\nu^{*} also optimizes the OCE stopping problem. Define the truncated quadratic utility by

u⁡(x)={x−x2/2,x≤1,1/2,x>1,u′​(x)=(1−x)+.u(x)=\begin{cases}x-x^{2}/2,&x\leq 1,\\ 1/2,&x>1,\end{cases}\qquad u^{\prime}(x)=(1-x)^{+}.

For X∈L2X\in L^{2}, any maximizing ν\nu satisfies 𝔼⁡[(1−X+ν)+]=1\mathbb{E}[(1-X+\nu)^{+}]=1. If X≤1+𝔼⁡[X]X\leq 1+\mathbb{E}[X] almost surely, then OCEu⁡(X)=𝔼⁡[X]−12​Var​(X)\operatorname{OCE}_{u}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]-\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Var}(X). The risk measure −OCEu-\operatorname{OCE}_{u} is convex but generally noncoherent. For nonnegative RtR_{t}, the transformed reward satisfies u⁡(−ν)≤u⁡(Rt−ν)≤1/2u(-\nu)\leq u(R_{t}-\nu)\leq 1/2 at each fixed ν\nu, so u⁡(Rt−ν)u(R_{t}-\nu) gives bounded weights in the pathwise gradient.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction distinguish structural results, conditional stationarity guarantees, and empirical comparisons.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Section 6 discusses limitations. Appendix A checks payoff moments and explains the policy-derivative and convergence assumptions.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: Sections 3 and 4.3 state the assumptions. Appendix B contains the proofs.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: The domains, policy architecture, threshold ranks, optimizer settings, evaluation protocol, and per-method tuning are described in the appendices.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [No]

  24. Justification: The manuscript does not provide a public code repository. Implementation and evaluation details are given in Appendix C.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: Appendix C specifies the training and evaluation protocol. Appendices D–H give settings for the additional experiments.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Tables report ten-seed means and population standard deviations. Appendix C specifies paired tests and the absence of multiplicity correction.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [No]

  39. Justification: The hardware and per-run times are reported in Appendix C. A complete project-wide compute total is not reported.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The research conforms with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: The introduction describes potential applications. Section 6 discusses the human and financial costs of inaccurate tail estimates in deployment.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper does not release data or models with a misuse risk.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [No]

  59. Justification: The baseline papers are cited, but licenses for all implementation components are not documented in this manuscript.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [N/A]

  64. Justification: The paper does not release new assets.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.
